Theoretical Foundations and Hypotheses How Referral Systems Can Disadvantage Women Referrals are important for securing jobs, promotions, and other forms of professional advancement.

Requesting a Larger Target Number of Referrals to Increase the Number of Women Referred We propose an intervention to increase referrals of women in male- dominated contexts: asking for a greater number of referrals, thereby modifying the choice architecture of the referral process (Thaler & Sunstein, 2021).
Thus, we hypothesize the following: Hypothesis 1: Requesting a greater number of referrals (e.g., four vs. two) will increase the total number of women referred.
Hypothesis 2: The effect of requesting a greater number of referrals on the total number of women referred will be mediated by an individual’s referral goal.
This possibility makes our hypotheses all the more important to test empirically.

In our context, we theorize asking for more referrals at the outset (vs. eliciting additional recommendations after an initial set has been generated) will increase the likelihood that people exhaust their repertoire of prototypical referrals (i.e., men in a male-dominated organizational context).
When people then continue making re- commendations, we predict they will transition to referring less prototypical candidates (i.e., women) as their referral list grows.

In other words, we propose that people will recommend women at a higher rate in “later” referral positions than in earlier ones (e.g., third or fourth referrals should be more likely to be women than ﬁrst or second referrals).
This leads to the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 3: Requesting a greater number of referrals (e.g., four vs. two) will increase the average likelihood that each individual referral is a woman.

Hypothesis 4: The effect of requesting a greater number of referrals on the average likelihood that each individual referred is a woman will be mediated by whether it was a later (e.g., third or later) referral versus an earlier (e.g., ﬁrst or second) referral.
All studies were preregistered on AsPredicted.org (however, we note that analyses relating to Hypotheses 3 and 4 were not preregistered).

Discussion Study 1 provides empirical support from a ﬁeld experiment for our theorizing that—consistent with what a goal-setting mechanism would predict—requesting a greater number of referrals increases the number of women referred in a male-dominated organizational context (Hypothesis 1).

However, the two manipulations did not interact, suggesting the beneﬁts of our more referrals intervention generalize across organizational environments that do (and do not) explicitly encourage recruiting from underrepresented populations.8 Our intervention did not increase the likelihood that an individual referral was a woman (Hypothesis 3).

Moreover, while requesting a greater number of referrals increased people’s likelihood of pro- viding later referrals, this did not mediate the relationship between the more referrals condition and the likelihood that a referral was a woman (Hypothesis 4).

Study S1 in our additional online material replicates these patterns in a second ﬁeld experiment with IDinsight that was procedurally identical but only had two conditions (more referrals vs. fewer referrals): Requesting more referrals signiﬁcantly boosted the number of women referred by 49% (supporting Hypothesis 1).
However, once again, we did not ﬁnd evidence for a prototype divergence mechanism (Hypotheses 3 and 4).

We also directly examine whether the more referrals condition causes participants to set more ambitious referral goals and whether this mediates the effect of condition assignment on the number of women referred (Hypothesis 2).

We conducted the same preregistered analyses as Study 1 and replicated our ﬁndings: Participants in the more referrals condition referred 62% more women (M = 0.99) than those in the fewer referrals condition (M = 0.61, b = 0.31, p < .001), further supporting Hypothesis 1.

Supporting Hypothesis 2, participants’ self-set goals signiﬁcantly mediated the relationship between assignment to the more referrals condition and the number of women they referred (b = 0.108, p < .001; 95% CI [0.045, 0.171]; see Figure 3).
Once again, we did not ﬁnd support for Hypothesis 3: There was a nonsigniﬁcant effect of assignment to the more referrals condition on the likelihood of referring a woman (b = −0.0001, p = .996).
This time, we found support for Hypothesis 4.

When interpolating such participants’ dependent measure, we found marginally signiﬁcant evidence of mediation such that the 90% CI (but not the 95% CI) for the indirect effect excluded 0 (b = 0.015, 90% CI [0.002, 0.027]).

Discussion Study 2 replicates the effect of requesting more referrals on increasing recommendations of women (Hypothesis 1) with a U.S. sample, establishing the robustness of our intervention across cultural contexts (Henrich et al., 2010).

This study also provides direct evidence for our theorized goal-setting mechanism: Participants who received a request to recommend more candidates subsequently set more ambitious referral goals, and these self-set goals mediated the effect of the more referrals condition on the number of women they referred (Hypothesis 2).
Our intervention again did not increase the likelihood of a given referral being a woman (Hypothesis 3).

However, we did ﬁnd support for Hypothesis 4: The more referrals condition increased the rate at which participants provided later referrals, and later referrals in turn were more likely to be women than earlier referrals.

Our intervention once again signiﬁcantly increased the number of women referred (by 88% in Study S2 and 25% in Study S3), further supporting Hypothesis 1 and conﬁrming this result holds across varied referral targets.
As in previous studies, we again did not ﬁnd evidence for Hypothesis 3.
Moreover, support for Hypothesis 4 was incon- sistent across these studies.

We did not ﬁnd any signiﬁcant evidence of mediation in Study S2, while in Study S3 we found signiﬁcant (or marginally signiﬁcant) evidence of media- tion in certain model speciﬁcations but not others.

We found a negative effect of assignment to the more referrals condition on the average rated competence of re- ferrals (b = −0.31, p < .001), which might be driven by participants believing the ﬁrst people who come to mind as potential referrals are also the most qualiﬁed (and often referring only those people in the fewer referrals condition but not the more referrals condition).

Across two ﬁeld experiments with an organization in India (Studies 1 and S1) and four online ex- periments with participants in the United States (Studies 2, S2, and S3 and Study S5, which is referenced further below), we found that requesting double the number of referrals (i.e., four vs. two, six vs. three) increased the number of women referred by 17%–88%.

We found support for the goal-setting mechanism in Study 2, while evidence for the pro- totype divergence account was inconsistent, with no evidence found in our ﬁeld experiments (Study 1 and Study S1) and mixed evidence across our online experiments (Study 2, Study S2, and Study S3).
